title: Routing splitter + edge-cache fallback design for mixed-latency POC
body:
Context and goal:
This doc captures a lightweight architecture proposal for a customer POC that needs sub-150ms p50 for conversational queries in EU region while keeping 99th percentile cost growth under 2.5x vs baseline hosted usage. Customer has mixed workloads: interactive chat (low tokens, user-facing, latency-sensitive), batch reranking (higher tokens, throughput-oriented), and occasional regulated flows that must be processed in-customer VPC (private).

Primary idea (the Splitter pattern):
Introduce a thin routing component (the 'splitter') placed logically in front of the Redwood runtime. The splitter evaluates each request on configurable rules and routes to one of: hosted-fast pool, dedicated-reserved pool, or private-onprem connectors. In front of the hosted pool we add an edge prefix cache layer (regional cache nodes) to short-circuit common prefixes and static system prompts. The cache supports stale-while-revalidate semantics to preserve p50 under transient misses.

Why this approach?
- Gives deterministic latency for small conversational requests by preferring hosted-fast when cache hits occur.
- Keeps regulated traffic on private connectors by routing by data classification tag.
- Uses dedicated capacity for sustained high-throughput or long-context batches to control costs.
- Allows progressive rollout: splitter rules are updated remotely without touching model pins or infra.

Routing decision inputs (examples):
- request_size_tokens (integer)
- auth_tier (enterprise, standard, guest)
- data_classification (public, confidential, regulated)
- latency_policy (low_p50, best_effort)
- prefix_signature (hash of prompt prefix + system prompt id)
- user_region (EU, NA, APAC)

Example rule table (simplified):
1) IF data_classification==regulated -> route: private-connector (VPC)
2) ELSE IF latency_policy==low_p50 AND prefix_signature cache hit -> route: hosted-edge-cache -> hosted-fast
3) ELSE IF request_size_tokens > 2048 OR inference_model==large-reranker -> route: dedicated-reserved
4) ELSE -> route: hosted-fallback

Edge cache semantics and TTLs:
- Keying: prefix_signature (system prompt id + first 64 tokens). Do not cache user-specific tokens (PII).
- TTLs: short TTLs (30s) for dynamic instructions, longer for static system prompts (5m).
- Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale for up to 200ms extra if backend miss would push p50 above target. Trigger background refresh to repopulate cache.
- Cache consistency: leverage versioned system prompt ids so prompt updates invalidate keys deterministically.

Failure modes and fallback behaviours:
- cache node down: splitter falls back to hosted-fast; record cache miss rates and route metrics
- hosted capacity saturated: fallback policy sends to dedicated if available, or degrade to best-effort hosted model variant (smaller quantized variant)
- private connector unreachable: queue with short retry window and fail closed for regulated flows (per customer policy) or fail open to dedicated if customer allowed

Observability & metrics to collect in POC:
- per-route p50/p95 latency, per-token cost (approx), and request success rate
- cache hit ratio by prefix_signature and effective p50 improvement from cache
- routing decision histogram (why each request went to target)
- fallback events (hosted->dedicated switch, private->dedicated) and time-to-fallback
- model quality regressions for fallback variants (sampled evals against golden prompts)

SLO targets for the POC (EU region):
- conversational requests (<=512 tokens): p50 < 150ms, p95 < 600ms
- batch/rerank (>=2048 tokens): throughput >= 150 reqs/s on dedicated pool (after warmup), p95 < 2.5s
- cache hit rate target: 40% for top 2k prefixes within first 2 weeks
- fallback correctness: <0.5% requests experiencing unintended fallback per day

Cost model tradeoffs (brief):
- Edge cache increases host cost (cache infra) but reduces per-token backend compute—best ROI when top prefixes are hot (~>20% of traffic).
- Dedicated pools incur committed cost but lower per-token billed cost for large contexts; good when steady high throughput exists.
- Private routing increases operational complexity; can be mitigated by using private connectors to hosted control plane for easier rollout.

Prototype implementation plan (4-week POC):
Week 0: alignment + access (customer sign-off on data classification and latency targets)
Week 1: Deliver minimal splitter (rule engine + metrics) and deploy edge-cache stub with synthetic cache keys. Integrate with Redwood hosted sandbox.
Week 2: Attach dedicated test pool, implement fallback policy, run synthetic traffic to validate fallback correctness and metrics.
Week 3: Run mixed workload soak with customer sample traffic, gather metrics, tune TTLs and rule thresholds.
Week 4: Run final performance/quality evaluation, produce recommendation memo (hosted-dominant vs dedicated-commit vs private migration).

Rollout knobs and quick experiments:
- Flip ratio: allow % of requests matching rule X to be randomly routed to alternate backend for quick A/B comparison (e.g., 10% to dedicated to compare cost/latency).
- TTL sweep: test 5s, 30s, 2m for dynamic prefixes to measure hit/refresh tradeoffs.
- Stale window tuning: incrementally increase stale-while-revalidate to see p50 improvement vs user-visible staleness.

Open questions for the workshop with customer:
- Are there regulatory constraints on caching request prefixes (even stripped of PII)? Any locale-specific retention rules?
- What SLA does customer want for regulated flows if private connector is temporarily unhealthy? (fail-open vs fail-closed)
- Acceptable quality delta for fallback model variants (quantized/smaller) — define sample prompts for automated evaluation.
- Can customer provide a representative sample of top N prompt prefixes or examples to seed cache?

Quick config snippet (pseudo YAML) for splitter rules:
- rules:
  - name: regulated-routing
    when: data_classification == "regulated"
    action: private_connector
  - name: cached-latency-path
    when: latency_policy == "low_p50" AND cache_hit == true
    action: hosted_fast
  - name: large-context
    when: request_size_tokens > 2048
    action: dedicated_pool
  - name: default
    action: hosted_fallback

Next steps (immediate):
- Review this design with SE-eng and infra (SRE) to identify infra requirements for edge cache nodes and metrics plumbing
- Prep a short demo harness to show cache hits vs misses and fallback transitions for the customer workshop
- Create a small eval suite (20 golden prompts) for monitoring quality when fallback to smaller models occurs

Notes to self / reminders:
- Keep the splitter stateless where possible; rely on consistent hashing of prefix_signature to keep cache locality and simplify scaling
- Instrument differential tracing through splitter so trace IDs follow request across edge cache -> hosted/dedicated/private paths
- Keep config dynamically reloadable from central config service so we can try rule tweaks during the POC without redeploys

References / useful links:
- Confluence: edge-splitter design page (linked above)
- SE-977: POC charter and constraints (linked above)
- PR 1428: initial router + metrics exporter implementation

Author note: this is a working draft intended for the upcoming customer workshop. Expect multiple iterations based on security/legal review and infra sizing feedback.
